title: Computer Network Infrastructure
short_description: Learn how an organization connects computers, servers and offices while maintaining efficient routes and minimizing infrastructure cost using graph algorithms.

real_world_context.problem: An organization needs to connect computers, servers and offices while maintaining efficient routes and minimizing infrastructure cost. Network engineers must trace which devices can be reached from a source, find low-latency routes between servers, decide which cables to install so every office is connected at the lowest cost, and keep every pair of devices able to communicate efficiently.
real_world_context.why_it_matters: Graph algorithms help organizations plan large networks efficiently, reduce cabling and infrastructure cost, and keep data flowing reliably between every device.

learning_objectives: Represent a computer network as an undirected graph using an adjacency list.
Traverse a network with Breadth-First Search (BFS) to map reachable devices.
Traverse a network with Depth-First Search (DFS) to explore connectivity.
Use Dijkstra's algorithm to find the lowest-latency route between two servers.
Use Kruskal's algorithm to connect all offices at minimum cabling cost.
Use Floyd-Warshall to compute efficient routes between every pair of devices.
prerequisites: Introduction to graphs and adjacency lists
completion_message: You have completed the Computer Network Infrastructure mission. You have learned how graph traversals, shortest-path algorithms and minimum-spanning-tree algorithms can be used to design cost-effective and efficient organization networks.
